method: One procedure, fitted on the public training pages only. (1) A glyph chain over the whole line, with the word space and the line end as ordinary symbols; each glyph is drawn given the four symbols before it, or, 6 times in 10, given only the two before it. It starts afresh at each line, from one start mark for a line that opens a paragraph and another for any other line. (2) The table drifts: the writer plans a book of 780 lines (15% of the manuscript's lines, the size of a sample of pages) and at each point uses counts from a window of 20 consecutive public pages that slides from the first page to the last as the book goes on (40 steps; the whole-text table is mixed in at weight 0.1). Paragraph-opening lines follow the same schedule at their own pace (their share of lines on the public pages, 14%). Lines written after the planned end use the last window. (3) Copying: at the start of a word, with probability 0.25, the writer takes one of the last 15 words written instead (on a paragraph-opening line, only words already on that line), preferring a word whose first glyph the chain allows after what was just written; 19 times in 20 it changes one glyph of it to another that the chain allows between its neighbours, otherwise it copies the word whole. No rule names a glyph, a word, a section or a Currier language, and none mentions pages being alike: the vocabulary of each stretch comes from the counts of the window in use. Lines holding a four-word run of the manuscript are redrawn. 'lines' are ordinary lines, 'first_lines' paragraph-opening lines. Two settings decide this fact, and both were chosen on the public practice split with it in view, which is the weakness of this attack. Exact copies: when 3 copies in 10 are whole words the singleton share is 0.58 to 0.65 (eight runs, fails); at 1 in 20 it is 0.66 to 0.68 (four runs, two of them passing). Context: drawing 6 glyphs in 10 from two symbols of context instead of four makes more new words and brings it to 0.697 here (manuscript 0.711, line 0.667), 0.692, 0.710, 0.702 for seeds 2 to 4 and 0.684 to 0.711 when fitted on every other public page only; all eight pass. A one-table chain of the same kind gives 0.67 to 0.68. What the procedure gives up for it: whole-word repetition. Its share of longer words already written on the page is 0.21 to 0.24 against the manuscript's 0.31 (the level sent as a fact under M-L2), and the setting with more exact copies that reaches 0.26 to 0.30 fails the singleton line. So this text meets the singleton share and, locally, the other established facts, but not the manuscript's combination of many once-only words with heavy reuse of a few common ones; no procedure tried here has both.
